analysis.one_liner: Bans commodity index funds from trading in oil and natural gas futures unless investors actually hedge.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 21 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for commodity index funds to buy or hold energy contracts like crude oil and natural gas on behalf of investors who have no real use for the fuel. These funds exist purely to profit from price changes, and the bill's authors argue their constant buying and rolling of contracts adds volatility and as much as a dollar per gallon to gasoline. Genuine hedgers—businesses that actually produce, refine, or burn fuel—are exempted. The bill went to the House Agriculture Committee, which oversees commodity trading, and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay energy prices—drivers filling their gas tanks, homeowners heating their homes, and airlines, truckers, and shippers buying fuel. The bill's findings say excessive index speculation may have added nearly $1.00 per gallon to gasoline, and claims that a ban would lower prices and reduce market volatility. Genuine physical hedgers keep full access to futures markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and households paying energy prices

how_it_helps.text: Bars commodity index funds from engaging in, accepting, or (after two years) holding energy commodity investments when any investor in the fund is an 'excluded investor'—someone with no bona fide hedging position in an energy commodity [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that speculators grew from 30% to 70% of open commodity futures contracts, index fund positions exceeded $160 billion by February 2012, and this 'rolling' of contracts adds hundreds of billions of dollars of trading volume monthly that the findings say raises retail prices, possibly by nearly $1.00 per gallon of gasoline [S3].

The definition of 'excluded investor' preserves full market access for bona fide hedgers—oil producers, refiners, airlines, and other businesses that actually use the commodities—so commercial users lose nothing [S2] [S3].

It builds on the Dodd-Frank Act, which had already directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to set position limits, by targeting index funds specifically rather than relying on agency rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms that sponsor and profit from commodity index funds lose a business line, and the institutions that invest in those funds—pension funds and universities, as the bill itself notes—lose an investment vehicle they use to diversify and to hedge against inflation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Index fund managers and their institutional investors

drawbacks.text: The bill's core premise—that index speculation drives up consumer fuel prices by as much as $1.00 per gallon—rests on congressional findings [S3], and many economists dispute how much passive index investment moves physical commodity prices; if the link is weak, the ban could restrict markets without delivering cheaper fuel.

A total ban goes further than the position limits Congress already ordered under Dodd-Frank [S3], and the bill itself notes that pension funds and universities are among the investors in these funds [S3], so the ban removes a diversification tool from ordinary savers whose retirement funds participate.
An outright prohibition on energy index trading could push that trading to offshore or less regulated markets, leaving US consumers exposed to the same price effects with less transparency.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the bill's causal claim is right, the benefit is large and broad: cheaper gasoline and heating fuel for every household and lower fuel costs for fuel-dependent businesses, at the price of closing one investment channel for wealthy institutions and the funds that serve them. The honest caveat is that the price-impact evidence is contested, so the ban's real-world benefit is uncertain even if its target—pure financial speculation in essential energy commodities—is easy to understand.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its General Farm Commodities and Risk Management Subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Markey introduced the bill on February 15, 2013, with 17 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture [S1] [S3] [S5].
The committee counts 21 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
On March 13, 2013, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management, and no further action of any kind is recorded for the rest of the 113th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and fund managers selling commodity index products keep the energy index business the bill would have shut down, and energy index funds kept their roughly $160 billion in positions. Consumers continue to pay whatever the market, including index speculation, charges at the pump.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Commodity index fund managers and sponsor banks

for.name: Rep. Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 21 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; all 21 were Democrats, including Reps. DeLauro, Grijalva, Schakowsky, and Watt.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 15, 2013 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in its General Farm Commodities and Risk Management Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Frank Lucas
against.what_they_did: As chairman during the 113th Congress, never brought the bill to markup or a vote, leaving it in subcommittee for the full two years.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill then died in a committee controlled by a Republican majority without any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Commodity index fund managers and the banks that sponsor them
industries.note: The bill would outlaw the core product—energy index funds sold to investors with no hedging position—including a market the bill's findings put at over $160 billion in net long positions by 2012. Their fee income depends on financial speculation in oil and gas contracts, which the bill says inflates consumer fuel prices.

industries.industry: Pension funds and universities invested in commodity indexes
industries.note: The bill's own findings identify these institutions as major index fund investors, and the ban would remove a diversification and inflation-hedging vehicle for their savers and endowments. They would also benefit as energy consumers if the bill's price-reduction claim holds.

industries.industry: Oil producers, refiners, and fuel-hedging businesses (airlines, truckers, shippers)
industries.note: Bona fide hedgers are exempt from the ban and keep full access to futures markets, while lower volatility and lower fuel prices would cut their biggest input costs.
